title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective Leaders
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Jain argues that the habits separating great leaders from good ones are counterintuitive rather than the expected traits of charisma, vision or assertiveness. He sets out seven: embracing failure as a stepping stone, leading authentically and with vulnerability, ignoring selectively to separate signal from noise, embracing imperfection through rapid experimentation, communicating transparently instead of hiding behind jargon, cultivating empathy alongside self-care, and embracing change. Each habit is illustrated with a well-known executive example (Jobs, Schultz, Nooyi, Dalio, Huffington, Conant, Hastings, and Kodak as a cautionary case). The author's own throughline is that the command-and-control archetype has given way to leaders who are imperfect, empathetic and unapologetically themselves. The piece leans on familiar anecdotes, but the framing and conclusions are the author's.
points: Effective leaders chase success too, but treat failure as an inevitable step toward it and build cultures that reward experimentation.
Selective ignorance is a skill: leaders who cannot separate signal from noise burn out themselves and their teams while still missing results.
Corporate jargon is often used to sugarcoat hard messages or dodge accountability; effective leaders choose open, candid communication even when it is uncomfortable.
Empathy for the team depends on a leader's own well-being: self-care and empathy go hand in hand rather than competing with results.
Failure to embrace change, as in Kodak's reluctance to leave film despite pioneering digital, leaves organizations obsolete.
quotes: While all those traits are nice to have, the habits that set the most effective leaders apart from the rest — the ones that truly matter — are often the most counterintuitive, surprising, yet incredibly inspiring.
Don’t get me wrong. Success is not a bad thing. In fact, the most effective leaders chase success too. The difference, however, is that they see failure as a stepping stone to success.
Highly effective leaders today are those who embrace vulnerability and authenticity. They are comfortable with their true selves, including their strengths, weaknesses, and insecurities.

Leaders who fail to differentiate what truly matters from the massive onslaught of information can get overwhelmed, and end up burning out themselves and their teams, while still not delivering the results.

The reality is that many leaders do this to mask (or sugarcoat) a difficult message, or to avoid taking accountability for what they are saying. Highly effective leaders, on the other hand, prioritize open and honest communication, even when it is uncomfortable or inconvenient.
However, effective leaders recognize that well-being is not a luxury, but a necessity for sustained success and resilience.
Leaders who embrace change allow themselves to stay agile and innovative, and position their organizations for long-term success.
